name: Scenario Planning
use_case: A technique that builds several internally consistent stories of how the future might unfold, usually by crossing the two most uncertain and most consequential driving forces into a grid of four worlds, then testing the current strategy against each. Best used for long-horizon commitments where forecasting a single number is dishonest, and the useful question is not what will happen but which choices survive across several plausible futures.
strengths: replaces a single false forecast with a set of testable futures
reveals which strategic choices are robust across all worlds
gives an organisation language for futures it otherwise refuses to discuss
the early-warning indicators keep working long after the workshop
weaknesses: expensive: real scenario work runs for weeks, not an afternoon
produces narratives that are easy to admire and hard to act on
picking only two axes discards uncertainties that later dominate
tempts groups toward a best case, worst case and a comfortable middle
use_cases: A government department is drafting a long-term policy, for example on transport or energy, and wants to check whether its options still work if technology and public attitudes move in very different directions.
An education ministry or a large school authority must commit to buildings, teacher training and curriculum for the next twenty years without knowing what role schools will play by then.
An energy or utility company has to plan capacity for a period in which regulation, technology and customer behaviour could each shift in either direction.
